extracted.intended_audience: general_news_readers interested in congressional hearings and the McCarthy-Army controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Writing or analyzing news coverage of televised Senate subcommittee hearings (procedural exchanges, testimony, and disputes). Focus is on accurately reporting rules, witness rights, and committee behavior in a public-investigation context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of points of order
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of order should not be used spuriously to interrupt testimony; the chair should refuse recognition when the practice is abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'The chair... lectured pers not propose to be interrupted by points of order that are not points of order.' Mundt said that if the practice of making “points of order” were to be abused, he would have to stop recognizing them. McCarthy countered he would interrupt when he found 'flagrant dishonesty on the part of a witness.' (Use of points of order must balance orderly proceedings and exposing dishonesty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No public accusation unless accused is present and can answer
rubrics_metrics.description: A person should not be publicly accused before the committee unless he is in the committee room and has an opportunity to 'step up and answer' immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'No one would be publicly accused unless he was in the committee room and had a chance to “step up and answer” immediately.' McCarthy had insisted on this rule when he chaired the investigating subcommittee; it is presented as a fairness standard for public accusations in hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of accused to be made a party, have counsel, and cross-examine
rubrics_metrics.description: If charges are made against an individual in the hearings, that person should be made a party to the investigation, permitted to engage counsel, and allowed to cross-examine witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from the text: 'If the charges were to be made against Schine, then Schine should be made a party to the investigation be permitted to engage counsel and cross-examine witnesses.' Chairman Mundt noted Schine's presence 'would be only fair.' This establishes procedural fairness: party status, counsel, and opportunity for rebuttal/cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert facts in questioning without introducing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioners should avoid phrasing queries as if disputed allegations are established facts unless supporting evidence has been introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reports McCarthy's objection: 'Jenkins might create the impression the questions were facts... McCarthy's complaint that Jenkins was asking questions as though they were facts, without any evidence being introduced to show they were facts.' Jenkins defended relevance, but the standard emphasized is that factual claims should be supported by evidence before being treated as fact in public hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid changing ground rules mid-hearing; enforce rules consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground rules for the hearing should not be altered halfway through the proceeding; rather, enforce existing rules more tightly if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original: 'Changing the ground rules halfway through the game... completely improper and dishonest.' Mundt said there would be no changes in the rules, just tighter enforcement. Symington suggested a rules change but McCarthy objected. Standard: ensure stability and fairness by not changing procedural rules midstream.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individuals from premature public release of committee information
rubrics_metrics.description: Information gathered by the committee should not be publicized in a way that prejudices individuals before they have had a chance to see or respond to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potter's concern: 'It would be unjust for the information to get... had a chance to see it.' He wrote to the Secretary of Defense because he thought the committee should have the report; the guidance implies avoiding leaks and ensuring fairness before public dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer persistent contradictory sworn statements for possible perjury investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: When witnesses make flat contradictions under oath, the committee should consider sending the record to the Justice Department for possible perjury action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McCarthy said the subcommittee 'has no choice but to send the entire record of the hearings to the Justice Department for possible perjury action.' Jackson noted the maximum penalty for perjury. Guidance: use the criminal-perjury process when sworn testimony contains serious, unresolved contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inspector-general reports and similar investigations as evidentiary basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcommittee questioning and allegations may be grounded on inspector-general findings; such reports should be offered into evidence when relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jenkins 'demanded that the [inspector general's] report be put into evidence.' Jenkins said his questions were based on what he had 'gleaned' from the inspector general's report. The implied standard: when relying on an investigative report, formally introduce it as evidence for transparency and fairness.
